## Proof

**Claim:** Yes. For every compact metric space $X$ and every $\epsilon > 0$, there exists a finite number $N(\epsilon, X)$ such that every $\epsilon$-equidistant subset $F \subset X$ satisfies $|F| \le N(\epsilon, X)$.

**Proof.**

Since $X$ is compact, $X$ is totally bounded. Hence for $\delta = \epsilon/2 > 0$, there exists a finite open cover of $X$ by balls of radius $\epsilon/2$:
$$X \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^{m} B(x_i,\, \epsilon/2), \qquad m < \infty.$$

Now let $F \subset X$ be any $\epsilon$-equidistant set. We show that each ball $B(x_i, \epsilon/2)$ contains **at most one** point of $F$.

Suppose for contradiction that two distinct points $p, q \in F$ both lie in $B(x_i, \epsilon/2)$. By the triangle inequality,
$$d(p,q) \;\le\; d(p, x_i) + d(x_i, q) \;<\; \tfrac{\epsilon}{2} + \tfrac{\epsilon}{2} \;=\; \epsilon.$$
But $p \neq q$ and $F$ is $\epsilon$-equidistant, so $d(p,q) = \epsilon$. This contradicts $d(p,q) < \epsilon$.

Therefore each of the $m$ balls contains at most one point of $F$, giving
$$|F| \;\le\; m \;<\; \infty.$$

It remains to note that the supremum is attained. The set of possible cardinalities
$$\mathcal{S} = \bigl\{\,|F| : F \subseteq X \text{ is } \epsilon\text{-equidistant}\,\bigr\}$$
is a nonempty (it contains $0$ and $1$, since $\emptyset$ and every singleton are vacuously $\epsilon$-equidistant) subset of the finite set $\{0, 1, \dots, m\}$. Being a finite nonempty set of integers, it attains its maximum. Set
$$N(\epsilon, X) \;=\; \max \mathcal{S}.$$
Then $N(\epsilon, X) \le m < \infty$, and by construction every $\epsilon$-equidistant $F \subset X$ satisfies $|F| \le N(\epsilon, X)$.

The bound genuinely depends on both $\epsilon$ and $X$: the covering number of $X$ at scale $\epsilon/2$ varies with the geometry of $X$ (e.g., $[0,1]$ vs. $S^1$ vs. higher-dimensional spheres admit $\epsilon$-equidistant sets of very different sizes for the same $\epsilon$). $\blacksquare$
